title.en: Death of a Naturalist and Why I Like the Hospital

hook.en: A boy's delight in frogspawn turns to fear; a patient finds an unexpected honesty in a hospital. Both poems show a moment when the way we see the world shifts.

objectives.en: Trace the change of mood in Death of a Naturalist
Explain the speaker's surprising view of the hospital
Comment on imagery and free verse in both poems

narration.en: A boy's delight in frogspawn turns to fear; a patient finds an unexpected honesty in a hospital. Both poems show a moment when the way we see the world shifts.

body.en: In two verse paragraphs, Heaney recalls his childhood on a farm in Northern Ireland. In the first, the rotting flax-dam teems with life; the boy happily collects frogspawn in jars, watches it grow and learns simple facts about frogs from his teacher, all told in a childlike, wondering voice. In the second, one hot day, the boy finds the dam invaded by croaking, angry frogs; their sounds and bodies now seem threatening and gross, and he runs away, sure that the frogspawn will take revenge if he touches it. His innocent love of nature dies: the "naturalist" in him is killed by a frightening, adult view of nature. Read the prescribed text itself; this guide is in our own words and quotes nothing.

points.en: Childlike voice of school nature lessons
Loss of innocence; nature's hidden power

He learns simple facts about frogs from his teacher
One hot day he hears a strange coarse croaking
He finds the dam invaded by angry-looking frogs
He runs away, sure the spawn will take revenge

explanation.en: The poem moves from delight to disgust; its turning point is the hot day when the frogs invade.

title.en: Why I Like the Hospital (Tony Hoagland)

body.en: Hoagland's free-verse poem, from a collection published after his death from cancer, gives a surprising reason for liking a hospital: there, people are allowed to stop pretending. Patients and families can be in a bad mood, show pain and fear, and face hard truths, such as how to tell children about a serious illness, without the polite masks of ordinary life. By contrast, everyday routines outside, like moving silently among strangers in a garage or lift, seem cold and false. The title is ironic: the poem is less a praise of hospitals than a criticism of a world that hides feeling. Read the prescribed text itself; this guide is in our own words and quotes nothing.

points.en: The hospital as a place of honesty
Irony in the title; illness, mortality, truth

problem.en: How does Heaney use the senses to show the change in the boy's feelings?

steps.en: In the first stanza, sounds and sights suggest abundance and warmth: buzzing, heat, jelly-like spawn in jars.
In the second, sounds become harsh and coarse, and the frogs' bodies are described as gross and threatening.
The same place is seen with new eyes: the senses carry the change from delight to disgust.
This shows how a child's innocent view gives way to fear.

answer.en: Heaney turns warm, delighted sensory detail into harsh, threatening detail to show the boy's loss of innocence.
